# Whether quantum advantage? New classical lower bounds for Max-Cut on large-girth 3-regular graphs

Every 3-regular graph of girth at least _g_ has a cut containing at least a fraction _Mg_ of its edges, and the best rigorous bounds at large girth are \(0.912\le lim_{g\rightarrow\infty} Mg\le 0.92386\). Lower bounds on _Mg_ follow from the performance of local algorithms: on a graph of girth \(g\ge 2p+2\) a depth-_p_ local algorithm sees the same tree around every edge, so its expected cut fraction on that tree bounds _Mg_ from below. We apply this strategy to the Variational Iterative Rotation Algorithm (VIRAL), a classical local algorithm, and evaluate it on the depth-_p_ tree for every even depth up to _p_=32. The resulting bounds exceed those recently obtained from the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for every \(p\ge 4\), by 0.005 to 0.011, and they extend the range of girths covered from _g_=36 to _g_=66. Notably, at _g_=66 we obtain \(M_{66}\ge 0.9127\) at 99.99999% confidence level, which raises the asymptotic lower bound from 0.912 to 0.9127.

_Introduction_ - The maximum cut of a graph _G_=(_V,E_) is the largest number of edges connecting the two sides of a bipartition of _V_ . Finding this cut is NP-hard even for 3-regular graphs [1]. The girth _g_ of a graph is the length of its shortest cycle. In a 3-regular graph of girth _g_, the ball of radius _d_ around any vertex contains no cycles whenever \(g\ge 2d+2\), and is then the same finite tree for every vertex, so all such graphs look alike locally and differ only globally, as illustrated in Fig. 1 for \(g\ge 6\). The question we address is what fraction of the edges an algorithm can guarantee to cut on these graphs. This motivates the following definition:

\(M_g=inf_{G\text{3-regular girth}(G)\ge g}\frac{\text{MaxCut}(G)}{|E(G)|}.\) (1)

The quantity _Mg_ is non-decreasing in _g_ and \(lim_{g\rightarrow\infty} Mg\) exists, but its value is not known. The best lower bound, \(lim_{g\rightarrow\infty} Mg\ge 0.912\), follows by combining the results of Refs. [2] and [3], as noted in [4]. The best upper bound comes from random 3-regular graphs, whose maximum cut fraction is asymptotically at most 0.92410 by the 1RSB bound conjectured in [5] and proven in [6], and at most 0.92386 by the tighter 2RSB bound of Ref. [7]. Thus

\(0.912\le lim_{g\rightarrow\infty} M_g\le 0.92386,\) (2)

and any progress on the lower bound must be made inside a window of width \(\Delta M\approx 0.012\).

All lower bounds on _Mg_ to date come from local algorithms, which assign a vertex to a side of the cut using only information up to distance _p_ from that vertex. On a graph of girth \(g\ge 2p+2\) the radius-_p_ neighborhood of every edge, defined below, is the same finite tree, as shown in Fig. 1 for \(g\ge 6\) and _p_=2. Therefore, the expected cut fraction of a local algorithm of depth _p_ is a single number that can be computed on the tree and bounds _Mg_ from below for all \(g\ge 2p+2\) [4]. The Quantum<tbc>

Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) [9] is an algorithm of this type and the depth-_p_ QAOA circuit is a local algorithm of radius _p_. A series of works evaluated the QAOA on large-girth regular graphs at increasing depth [10, 11], culminating in \(Mg\ge 0.8971\) for \(g\ge 36\) from _p_=17 [4]. Classical local algorithms have been compared with the QAOA. At depth one [12] and two [13] simple classical rules outperform the QAOA for every degree, and numerical experiments on small random 3- regular graphs suggest the same at larger depth [14]. On large-girth graphs, however, the picture is different: at degree three the explicit vector algorithm of Thompson, Parekh, and Marwaha [8], whose guarantees are known at every depth, falls behind the QAOA for \(p\ge 7\) [4] (see  I). We recently introduced the Variational Iterative Rotation Algorithm (VIRAL) [15], a classical local algorithm in which every vertex carries a unit vector that is rotated _p_ times by angles set by its neighbors. <tbc>dom 3-regular graphs with 10<sup>6</sup> vertices, we numerically found that VIRAL cuts more edges than the QAOA at every depth \(p\ge 4\) and its expected cut fraction extrapolates to 0.9231(5) for \(p\rightarrow\infty\), very close to the upper bound in Eq. (2) \[15\]. That benchmark, however, compares VIRAL on finite random graphs against the QAOA on the tree, and establishes no bound. Indeed, a random 3-regular graph has short cycles, which at _N_=10<sup>6</sup> enter the radius-_p_ neighborhood of a typical edge already for \(p\unknown 9\), so a cut fraction measured there is not a bound on _M<sub>g</sub>_.

Here we evaluate VIRAL on the tree itself, which makes the comparison with the QAOA well defined and turns its cut fractions into bounds on _M<sub>g</sub>_. We estimate the expected cut fraction on the depth-_p_ tree by sampling the seeds, with 10<sup>7</sup> samples for every even \(p\le 32\). The deepest computation involves \(4\cdot 2^{32}\approx 1.7\times 10^{10}\) vertices per sample. The resulting lower bounds on _M<sub>g</sub>_ are reported in  I and plotted in Fig. 2. They exceed the QAOA bounds and those of Ref. \[8\] at equal depth for every \(p\ge 4\), and they extend the range of girths covered from _g_=36 to _g_=66. At _g_=66 the estimate _c_<sub>VIRAL</sub>(32)=0.913183(89) lies 13 standard errors above the asymptotic record in Eq. (2), and the rigorous bound is \(M_{66}\ge 0.91271\) at 99.9999% confidence level.

_Setup_ - VIRAL assigns to every vertex _i_ a classical spin, i.e., a unit vector \(\mathbf{s}_i=(s_i^x,s_i^y,s_i^z)\in S^2\), and updates<tbc>

<tbc>all spins synchronously for _p_ layers as

\(\mathbf{s}_i(n+1)=R_x(\beta_n)R_z\big(\gamma_nh_i(n)\big)\mathbf{s}_i(n),n=0,\dots,p-1,h_i(n)=\sum_{j\in\partial i}s_j^z(n),\text{(3)}\)

where \(\partial i\) is the set of neighbors of _i_, \(R_z(\theta)\) and \(R_x(\theta)\) are rotations by angle \(\theta\) about the _z_ and _x_ axes, and \(\beta_n,\gamma_n\) are fixed real parameters \[15\]. The initial condition is<tbc>

\(\mathbf{s}_i(0)=\big(\mathrm{cos}\alpha,0,\epsilon_i\mathrm{sin}\alpha\big),\) (4)

<tbc>with a fixed angle \(\alpha\) and independent fair random seeds \(\epsilon_i\in\{-1,+1\}\). After the last layer each spin is thresholded,

\(\sigma_i(p)=\mathrm{sign}(s_i^z(p)),\) (5)

and the cut is the set of edges with \(\sigma_u\neq\sigma_v\). The 2_p_+1 parameters \((\alpha,\beta_0,\dots,\beta_{p-1},\gamma_0,\dots,\gamma_{p-1})\) are trained once, as described below, and then frozen, so that the same parameters are used on every graph. The seeds are essential. On a regular graph, spins that start identical remain identical under Eq. (3), because every vertex sees the same field, _h<sub>i</sub>=h_ for every _i_, and no edge would ever be cut. The seeds break this symmetry and are the only source of randomness in the algorithm. The initial condition in, given by expression (4), has a semiclassical origin. In the truncated Wigner approximation of the QAOA, the unitaries become the classical rotations of Eq. (3) and the initial state \(|+\rangle\) becomes a set of classical spins with (Gaussian) random transverse components, whose width plays the role of \(\hbar\) \[16\]. The seeds \(\epsilon_i\) are the minimal form of this noise: the transverse component has fixed amplitude \(\mathrm{sin}\alpha\) and only its sign is random. In Ref. \[16\] we found that the semiclassical dynamics with a tuned noise level reaches lower energies than the exact QAOA at every depth, and that replacing the Gaussian noise by the seeds and reoptimizing \(\alpha\) together with the angles, which is VIRAL, improves the convergence of the energy to the ground-state value from log(_p)/p_ to 1_/p_. The optimal noise level found there vanishes as \(p\rightarrow\infty\). In accordance, the trained amplitude for MaxCut also decreases with depth, from \(\alpha=0.46\) at _p_=2 to \(\alpha=0.018\) at _p_=32.

Next we show that VIRAL is local, in the sense that whether an edge is cut depends only on a bounded portion of the graph around it. The graph enters Eq. (3) only through the neighbor sets \(\partial i\). Consider the graph of Fig. 1 with _p_=2 and let us trace the computation of \(\sigma_u=\mathrm{sign}(s_u^z(2))\) backwards, as in Fig. 3. By Eq. (3), **s**_<sub>u</sub>_(2) is computed from **s**_<sub>u</sub>_(1) and from the field \(h_u(1)=s_v^z(1)+s_{a_1}^z(1)+s_{a_2}^z(1)\), so it needs the spins at time 1 of _u_ and of its three neighbors, and the only edges involved are the three edges incident to _u_. Each of these four spins at time 1 is in turn computed from the seed of its own vertex and from the seeds of the three neighbors of that vertex. <tbc>only edges involved are those incident to _u,v,a_<sub>1</sub>_,a_<sub>2</sub> (the vertices within distance 1 of _u_). The leaves _a_<sub>11</sub>_,...,b_<sub>22</sub> enter only through their seeds and their states at times 1 and 2 are never needed, so which other vertices a leaf is connected to does not matter. In particular, the dashed edge of Fig. 1 plays no role. Repeating the argument for \(\sigma_v\), the pair \((\sigma_u,\sigma_v)\) is a function of the seeds of the 14 vertices within distance 2 of _u_ or _v_, computed using only the solid edges of Fig. 1.

The same unfolding applies at any depth _p_ and on any 3-regular graph _G_, since each layer brings in the seeds of vertices one step farther away and the edges involved are those incident to the vertices whose state at some time \(n\ge 1\) is needed. Thus, the pair \((\sigma_u,\sigma_v)\) at an edge (_u,v_) is a function of the seeds of the vertices within distance _p_ of _u_ or _v_, computed using only the edges incident to the vertices within distance _p_-1 of _u_ or _v_. We call this set of vertices and edges the radius-_p_ neighborhood of the edge (_u,v_). Nothing outside it can change whether the edge is cut or not.

Now let _G_ have girth \(g\ge 2p+2\). Then the radius-_p_ neighborhood of any edge contains no cycle, and is thus a tree. Since _G_ is 3-regular, it is always the same tree, consisting of the endpoints _u,v_ joined by the root edge, each carrying a complete binary tree of depth _p_, as in Fig. 1 for _p_=2. Level _q_ of this tree is the set of vertices at distance _q_ from the nearer of _u_ and _v_, and contains 2<sup>_q_+1</sup> vertices for _q_=0_,...,p_. In total the number of<tbc>

<tbc>vertices in the tree is

\(N_p=2+4+\cdots+2^{p+1}=4\cdot 2^p-2.\) (6)

Since the algorithm sees nothing beyond this tree, and the seeds on it are i.i.d., the joint probability of \((\sigma_u,\sigma_v)\) is identical for every edge of every 3-regular graph of girth at least 2_p_+2. We call

\(c_\mathrm{VIRAL}(p)=\mathrm{Prob}\big[\sigma_u\neq\sigma_v\big],\) (7)

where (_u,v_) is the root edge of the depth-_p_ tree decorated with i.i.d. seeds, the value of the algorithm on the tree. It is a property of the 2_p_+1 parameters alone, not of any specific graph. Note that the tree itself is bipartite, so its own maximum cut fraction is 1, attained by the alternating 2-coloring of its vertices. This coloring, however, is not a local function of the seeds. The reason is that the outputs of a local algorithm at two vertices at distance \(\ell\) of the 3-regular tree have a correlation that decays as \(2^{\ell/2}\) \[17\], while the 2-coloring has correlation \((-1)^\ell\). Consistently, Eq. (10) below shows that _c_<sub>VIRAL</sub>(_p_) never exceeds \(\mathrm{lim}_{g\rightarrow\infty} M_g\le 0.92386\).

_From the tree to a bound on M<sub>g</sub>_ - Let us consider any 3-regular graph _G_ of girth \(g\ge 2p+2\) and run the algorithm on it with the fixed parameters and fresh i.i.d. seeds \(\epsilon\). The output \(\sigma(\epsilon)\) is a random cut of _G_, whose

<tbc>expectation is

\(\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{\mathrm{cut}(\sigma(\epsilon))}{|E|}\right]=\frac{1}{|E|}\sum_{(u,v)\in E}\mathrm{Prob}\big[\sigma_u\neq\sigma_v\big]=c_\mathrm{VIRAL}(p).\) (8)

Now, a random variable is at least as large as its mean with positive probability and, since there are finitely many seed configurations, some \(\epsilon^*\) satisfies \(\mathrm{cut}(\sigma(\epsilon^*))/|E|\ge c_\mathrm{VIRAL}(p)\), and the maximum cut is at least as large, i.e.<tbc>

\(\frac{\mathrm{MaxCut}(G)}{|E(G)|}\ge c_\mathrm{VIRAL}(p).\) (9)

<tbc>Note that nothing about _G_ was used except its degree and its girth, so Eq. (9) holds for every graph in the class defining _M<sub>g</sub>_, and thus for their infimum. Together with the fact that _M<sub>g</sub>_ is non-decreasing in _g_ we conclude that

\(\mathrm{lim}_{g\rightarrow\infty} M_g\ge M_{2p+2}\ge c_\mathrm{VIRAL}(p).\) (10)

This is precisely the argument by which Farhi _et al._ turn a QAOA expectation value into a bound on _M<sub>g</sub>_ \[4\]. The only difference is that the expectation in Eq. (8) is over classical random seeds rather than over a quantum state.

Two consequences follow. First, the bound is constructive, in that on any 3-regular graph of girth at least 2_p_+2, one run of the algorithm costs _O(p|E_|) operations and produces a cut whose expected fraction is _c_<sub>VIRAL</sub>(_p_), with the parameters precomputed once for each _p_. Second, _c_<sub>VIRAL</sub>(_p_) is a classical expectation that we estimate by sampling the seeds, whereas the QAOA expectation of Ref. \[4\] is evaluated exactly by tensor-network methods. Each sample returns one bit, i.e., whether the root edge is cut, so from _S_ samples with _K_ cut events the estimate \(\hat{c}=K/S\) has standard error \(\sigma=\sqrt{\hat{c}(1-\hat{c})/S}\). For _S_=10<sup>7</sup> the estimate is Gaussian to high accuracy, and the probability that it exceeds the true value by more than \(5.2\sigma\) is 10<sup>-7</sup>. Hence

\(L=\hat{c}-5.2\sigma\) (11)

is a lower bound on _c_<sub>VIRAL</sub>(_p_) at 99.9999% confidence level.  I reports the exact binomial bound at the same level, which agrees with Eq. (11) to within 10<sup>-6</sup>. Since Eq. (10) holds for every value of _c_<sub>VIRAL</sub>(_p_), the statement \(M_g\ge L\) for all \(g\ge 2p+2\) holds at the same confidence level.

_Computing c_<sub>VIRAL</sub>(_p_) - The depth-_p_ tree is not a truncation of the infinite tree but the exact object to consider, in that nothing beyond it reaches the root edge. We draw the _N<sub>p</sub>_ i.i.d. seeds, run Eq. (3) on the tree, and record the single bit \(\unknown[\sigma_u\neq\sigma_v]\). Then _c_<sub>VIRAL</sub>(_p_) is the mean of this bit over _S_=10<sup>7</sup> independent draws. In particular, at _p_=2 no sampling is needed: the tree has 14 vertices, as in Fig. 1, so all 2<sup>14</sup>=16384 seed configurations can be run through Eq. (3) one by one, and we find that 12380 of them cut the root edge. The exact<tbc>

<tbc>value _c_<sub>VIRAL</sub>(2)=12380/16384=0.755615 agrees with the sampled one in  I within 1.2 standard errors.

_Parameters_ - The 2_p_+1 parameters are those obtained in Ref. \[15\] by training VIRAL on random 3- regular graphs, and are used here unchanged \[18\]. We computed them for even _p_ only, which is why  I lists even depths. Each training instance consists of a random 3-regular graph with _N_=10<sup>6</sup> vertices and one fixed realization of the seeds. The cost function is the continuous energy \(\sum_{(i,j)\in E}s_i^z(p)s_j^z(p)\) averaged over 10 instances, whose gradient with respect to \((\alpha,\beta_n,\gamma_n)\) is computed exactly by backpropagation through the _p_ layers of Eq. (3). Two remarks are in order: first, the same parameters are used on every graph, as the argument leading to Eq. (10) requires; second, they are not optimal for the tree, since they were optimized on graphs with cycles. Therefore, every value in  I is a conservative estimate of what VIRAL can guarantee at that depth, in that parameters optimized on the tree itself can only do better.

_Discussion_ - Evaluated on the depth-_p_ tree, VIRAL yields rigorous lower bounds on _M<sub>g</sub>_ for every girth up to 66. At equal depth they exceed the QAOA bounds by 0.005 to 0.011 and those of Ref. \[8\] at every \(p\ge 4\), and at _g_=66 they pass 0.912, a value previously reached only in the limit of infinite girth. Therefore, the asymptotic lower bound in Eq. (2) becomes

\(0.9127\le\mathrm{lim}_{g\rightarrow\infty} M_g\le 0.92386.\) (12)

The bounds are constructive, and the algorithm attaining them runs in time linear in the number of edges.

These results bear on the question of quantum advantage for local algorithms. Ref. \[4\] found that on 3-regular graphs the QAOA beats the best classical local algorithm with a provable guarantee for \(g\ge 16\), and Ref. \[19\] has recently extended this comparison to Max-_k_-Cut on _d_- regular graphs, where the QAOA overtakes an improved vector algorithm for \(g\ge 20\) at every _k_ and _d_ considered, an apparent quantum advantage at moderate girth. The tree value _c_<sub>VIRAL</sub>(_p_) is a guarantee of the same kind, and at _k_=2 and _d_=3 it exceeds the QAOA value at every even depth \(p\ge 4\) up to 32, in particular at every girth where Ref. \[4\] found the QAOA ahead of the classical algorithms. In this case, therefore, the advantage does not exist. Whether the same holds at higher degree and for \(k\ge 3\) is a natural next test. The same conclusion was reached on the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick (SK) model, which governs the large-degree limit of Max-Cut on regular graphs \[11\]. There VIRAL outperforms the QAOA at every depth \[15\], and so does the semiclassical limit of the QAOA itself \[16\]. In both cases, the dense SK model and sparse 3-regular graphs, the quantum fluctuations of the QAOA are not a resource. Their classical remnant, i.e. the random seeds, is all the dynamics needs, and it does better without the rest.

Finally, we note that the increments _c_<sub>VIRAL</sub>(_p_)-_c_<sub>VIRAL</sub>(_p_-2) are still decreasing at _p_=32 and the<tbc>

<tbc>present data do not determine the limit \(p\rightarrow\infty\). How much of the remaining gap to 0.92386 a local algorithm can close is an open question.
